questions.title: How does the Cayley transform ensure the orthogonality of $\bm{R}$?
questions.question_body: In the section on Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT), the authors mention that they employ Cayley parameterization, defined as $\bm{R}=(\bm{I}+\bm{Q})(\bm{I}-\bm{Q})^{-1}$ where $\bm{Q}$ is a skew-symmetric matrix ($\bm{Q}=-\bm{Q}^\top$). I understand that this is used to ensure $\bm{R}$ remains orthogonal throughout the training process, but I am struggling with the mathematical intuition. How does the skew-symmetry of $\bm{Q}$ specifically guarantee that $\bm{R}^\top \bm{R} = \bm{I}$?

questions.title: Why is the butterfly structure considered 'dense' while the block-diagonal structure is not?
questions.question_body: I am confused about the terminology used in the paper. Both the block-diagonal structure in original OFT and the butterfly structure in BOFT use sparse matrices to reduce the number of parameters. However, the paper states that the block-diagonal structure cannot construct a dense matrix $\bm{R}$, whereas BOFT is designed to generate a 'dense orthogonal matrix' via factorization. If the individual factors $\tilde{\bm{B}}^b_{(d,j)}$ are sparse, in what sense is the resulting matrix $\bm{R}$ actually dense?

questions.title: How does the 'information transmission' view map to matrix multiplication?
questions.question_body: The authors introduce a grid-structured graph where $\bm{B}_i$ is viewed as the connectivity matrix from level $i$ to $i+1$. They state that for $\bm{R} = \bm{B}_m \dots \bm{B}_1$ to be dense, every node in the first level must have a path to every node in the $(m+1)$-th level. I'm trying to reconcile this with linear algebra: does this imply that the product of these sparse matrices results in a matrix where almost all entries $R_{ij}$ are non-zero, and how does the butterfly topology specifically satisfy this 'dense connectivity' requirement more efficiently than other sparse patterns?

questions.title: Why does preserving the spectral norm of $\bm{W}^0$ benefit training stability?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that because $\bm{R}$ is orthogonal, the finetuned weights $\bm{R}\bm{U}\bm{\Sigma}\bm{V}^\top$ preserve the largest singular value (spectral norm) of the pretrained weight matrix $\bm{W}^0$. The authors claim this 'greatly benefit[s] training stability and generalization.' I don't quite understand the mechanism here. Why does keeping the spectral norm constant prevent the training from becoming unstable compared to a method like LoRA, which uses additive updates?

questions.title: What is the intuition behind the 'multiplicative Dropout' in BOFT?
questions.question_body: The paper proposes a multiplicative Dropout that replaces randomly selected butterfly components or diagonal blocks with identity matrices, rather than using standard dropout which sets elements to zero. Is this necessary because setting elements of an orthogonal matrix to zero would destroy the orthogonality property? If we used standard dropout on the skew-symmetric matrix $\bm{Q}$ instead, would that achieve a similar effect without breaking the orthogonal constraint?

questions.title: Regarding the trade-off between expressivity and regularity in BOFT
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 and the associated simulations suggest that BOFT is significantly more expressive than block-diagonal OFT, meaning it can better approximate a general orthogonal matrix. However, the authors later state that 'better expressiveness does not always lead to better performance' and that the key is the trade-off between expressivity and regularity. If BOFT allows us to access a larger subset of the orthogonal group, why would that not always be an advantage? In what way could too much expressivity lead to worse generalization in the context of finetuning?
